claims.text: Rapid quenching from the melt or a high temperature will reduce the grain size of the magnetic high-entropy alloy.
Reducing grain size increases the density of domain-wall pinning sites.
Increasing the density of domain-wall pinning sites increases the coercive field.
Conventional annealing produces a relatively coarse-grained baseline alloy.
Processing in an inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during rapid quenching.
The predicted coercivity effect requires substantial grain refinement without undesired phase transformations.
A reduction in average grain size increases grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries act as effective pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Greater grain-boundary density obstructs domain-wall motion.
Obstructing domain-wall motion raises the energy barrier for magnetization reversal.
A higher energy barrier for magnetization reversal increases coercivity relative to a conventionally annealed sample.
The rapidly quenched, fine-grained sample will have a statistically significant higher coercive field than the coarse-grained baseline.
The effect should hold when the composition and processing conditions produce a stable fine-grained microstructure.
High concentrations of nonmagnetic elements may prevent the predicted coercivity trend.
Compositions that undergo phase separation may not follow the predicted coercivity trend.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis conditions the effect on successful formation of a stable fine-grained microstructure, but the falsification rule also treats failure to produce grain refinement as falsification. Failure of the processing protocol to create the proposed mediator would not by itself falsify the claimed grain-size-to-coercivity relationship.
